query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) ZrB2-AlFeNiCoCr cermets at 1500°C improves resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by optimizing binder fluidity and densification, which enhances grain bonding and minimizes pore connectivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixed powder consisting of high-purity ZrB2 (1–5 μm) and 30% AlFeNiCoCr high-entropy-alloy binder (from equimolar Al, Fe, Ni, Co, and Cr powders, ethanol-milled and vacuum-dried).
generation.intervention: Consolidate the cermets by SPS specifically at 1500°C.
generation.conditions: SPS under vacuum at 50 MPa with a heating rate of approximately 200°C/min and a 5-minute hold; subsequent corrosion tests involve immersion in molten aluminum at 700°C for periods up to 12 days and wear tests using a Si3N4 ball under a 10 N load at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: At 1500°C, the liquid high-entropy-alloy binder uniformly infiltrates pores and strongly connects ZrB2 grains, leading to the highest relative density (~97.71%) and a compact microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced binder fluidity at 1500°C promotes effective pore filling and grain bonding, which minimizes pathways for molten Al penetration. This in turn suppresses ZrB2 grain detachment, reduces formation of Al-rich reaction products, and improves hardness and fracture toughness, thereby increasing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to cermets sintered at 1300, 1400, or 1600°C, the samples sintered at 1500°C should exhibit superior density, increased hardness and fracture toughness, lower molten-aluminum corrosion rates, reduced wear volume, and more stable friction behavior—even achieving fracture toughness values exceeding those of pure ZrB2 ceramics.
generation.baseline: Cermets processed at 1300°C, 1400°C, and 1600°C, with pure ZrB2 ceramics (reference fracture toughness ~4.5 MPa·m^1/2) serving as benchmarks.
generation.boundary: Results apply specifically to the 30% binder ZrB2-AlFeNiCoCr composition processed under the described SPS parameters, with performance validated under molten-Al exposure at 700°C for up to 12 days and the specified room-temperature wear test.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding long-term performance beyond 12 days and the scalability of these results to variations in binder composition or different SPS configurations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare ZrB2-AlFeNiCoCr cermets using SPS at four different temperatures: 1300°C, 1400°C, 1500°C, and 1600°C. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/EDS and XRD. Evaluate relative density via Archimedes method, conduct Vickers hardness and indentation fracture toughness tests, assess molten-Al corrosion performance by immersing samples in molten aluminum at 700°C for intervals up to 12 days, and perform ball-on-disc wear tests under a 10 N load at room temperature.
measurements: Thickness-loss corrosion rate in molten Al
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cermets sintered at 1500°C do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in microstructural density, mechanical properties, and reduced corrosion as well as wear performance compared to samples sintered at 1300°C, 1400°C, and 1600°C, then the hypothesis is falsified.
